text: Every quantum algorithm you'll build is a sequence of matrices multiplying a state vector, and the three Pauli gates are the simplest, most fundamental matrices in that toolbox. Get comfortable with X, Y, and Z here, because every gate in the rest of this course is either built from them or compared against them.

Each Pauli gate is a fixed 2 by 2 unitary matrix with no adjustable parameter. X is 0, 1, 1, 0. Y is 0, negative i, i, 0. Z is 1, 0, 0, negative 1. All three are Hermitian and unitary, and all three square to the identity matrix, meaning applying any one of them twice brings you right back to where you started.

X swaps the amplitudes of ket-zero and ket-one — exactly what a classical NOT gate does, which is why it's called the quantum NOT. Y does the same bit flip but attaches a phase: Y on ket-zero gives i times ket-one, and Y on ket-one gives negative i times ket-zero. Since the magnitude of i squared is 1, measurement probabilities are completely unaffected. But that phase isn't nothing — it's exactly the ingredient that interference-based algorithms, starting next chapter, are built from.

Z is the odd one out: it leaves ket-zero completely alone and multiplies ket-one by negative 1 — no bit flip, only a sign change. Apply Z to the equal superposition, 1 over root 2 times ket-zero plus 1 over root 2 times ket-one, and you get 1 over root 2 times ket-zero minus 1 over root 2 times ket-one. The state vector changed, but squaring each amplitude's magnitude gives the same 0.5, 0.5 measurement probabilities before and after. Relative phase is invisible to a lone measurement, but it is not nothing — it becomes observable the moment that qubit meets a gate that can turn phase into amplitude, which is exactly what's coming next.
Next lesson introduces the Hadamard gate — the first gate in this course that genuinely creates superposition out of a definite classical-looking state.
